statement: Point A is 3 cm above a straight line and point B is 5 cm above it, with A and B 10 cm apart horizontally. A path runs from A to the line and then to B. What is its shortest length?

choices.misconception: I used the horizontal distance alone and ignored the heights entirely.
I reflected A but used the difference of the heights rather than their sum.

choices.text: the square root of 34 plus the square root of 50
choices.misconception: I bounced off the point of the line halfway between A and B, assuming the middle is best.
I went straight down from A, along the line and straight up to B, adding 3 + 10 + 5.

hints: Reflect one of the points in the line.
Reflecting A across the line turns the bent path into a straight one of the same length, so the shortest path is the straight distance from the reflected point to B.
The reflection of A sits 3 cm below the line, so it is 8 cm vertically and 10 cm horizontally from B.

solutions.reliable: Reflecting A in the line sends it 3 cm below, and any path A to line to B has the same length as the corresponding path from the reflection to B. The shortest such path is straight, with length the square root of 10 squared plus 8 squared, which is the square root of 164. The transferable idea: a reflection straightens a bounce, so the shortest bent path becomes a plain distance.
solutions.elegant: The square root of 164 is 2 times the square root of 41, exactly twice the box-unfolding answer in the level below.

whyOnTest: The reflection trick is the only way to make a shortest bouncing path calculable, and the unreflected height difference is the predictable trap.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
